8.9.1. iLock_Geography.geo_algorithms.prot.nodeIndexIter2ProtectionObjects¶

iLock_Geography.geo_algorithms.prot.nodeIndexIter2ProtectionObjects(railyard, userProtectionObjectTypes, nodeIndexIter)¶

Given a set of nodes with incoming edges specified, calculate a set of railyard objects (signals and switches) protecting these nodes.

Only trailing signals and switches (as seen from the protected nodes) are used as potential protection objects. For each node index the first candidate (the closest) found will be used, except in the case when two node indices try to use the same trailing switch as protection object, and the switch is required to be in conflicting positions. In that case the search for protection objects for the two node indices continues beyond the switch. Note that this is the main reason why this function takes a group of node indices, instead of a single node index.

If no protection object is found for a certain node index, the search in that direction ends in a degree 1 node. All degree 1 nodes found in this way are returned to the caller.

Parameters:
  • railyard (IRailyard) – The railyard we are examining.
  • userProtectionObjectTypes ({str}) – The user types (subtypes of the base types Signal and/or Switch) of the objects that are to be used for protection.
  • nodeIndexIter (Iterable(NodeIndex)) – The node indices that are to be protected. The index defines the incoming direction we want to protect.
Return type:

({IRailyardObject}, {INode}, {NodeIndex}, {IRailyardObject:enum(1, 2)})
Returns:

A 4-tuple (protObj, endNodes, processedNI, switchPos) containing:

  • protObj: all protection objects found,
  • endNodes: all end nodes corresponding to missing protection
    objects,
  • processedNI: all node indices that were searched (including the
    ones given in the argument nodeIndexIter), and
  • switchPos: for each protection object of switch type, the
    leg index which corresponds to the safe switch position.
